Right, so expecting the auth controller and auth routes to pick up the forgot/reset endpoints, the User model to grow a reset token field plus expiry, mailer getting wired up to actually send the link, and a new reset password page on the client with its route added. That's already six if routes.jsx and the auth api wrapper both need touching too, so plausible split is auth controller, auth routes, User model, mailer, a new ResetPassword page, and routes.jsx.

The thing I'd watch for is whether crypto.js gets reused for generating the token or whether they roll their own inline in the controller, and whether the reset token actually gets hashed before it's stored or just saved raw on the user document.
Let me put that differently. Work it from what you already know about the repo, and say what you would expect - I will check it against the real change once the agent is done.

Given crypto.js already exists as a lib, I'd expect the agent to use it for generating and hashing the reset token rather than inventing new logic, since that's the established pattern here for anything security-adjacent. And given mailer.js is already separated out as its own lib rather than inline in the controller, I'd expect the forgot-password flow to call into it the same way, so the six files are probably the auth controller, auth routes, User model for the token and expiry fields, a new ResetPassword page on the client, routes.jsx to register it, and either the auth api wrapper or Login.jsx to add the forgot-password link in.

Agent needs you. I will wait.

Both, really, but if I had to pick one as the more likely of the six over the client wrapper, I'd say server/routes/auth.js, since the new endpoints have to be declared there regardless, whereas the client api/auth.js only needs touching if the new page doesn't just inline its own fetch calls.

Got it, your file picks are locked in.

Now, forgetting about which files are involved: walk me through what should happen step by step, starting the moment the user clicks "forgot password", through to the moment they're successfully logged in with a new password. What has to happen at each stage for this to work correctly?

User clicks forgot password, lands on a form asking just for their email, submits it, and the server looks up that user but responds with the same generic "if that email exists, we've sent a link" message either way so you can't use this to enumerate accounts. If the user does exist, the server generates a random token, hashes it before storing it on the user document alongside an expiry timestamp maybe fifteen minutes to an hour out, then mails the unhashed version embedded in a link pointing at the reset password page on the client.

User clicks the link, lands on a reset page that pulls the token out of the URL, and shows a simple new-password form, nothing happens with the token yet until they submit. On submit the client sends the token plus new password to the server, which hashes the incoming token, looks up a user with that hashed token where the expiry hasn't passed, and if that all lines up it hashes the new password with whatever the existing signup flow uses, saves it, and crucially clears the reset token and expiry fields so the link can't be reused. Then either the server logs them in directly by issuing a session or JWT the same way login does, or it just redirects to the login page with a success message and makes them log in fresh with the new password, I'd guess the latter since it's simpler and I didn't see a shared "issue session" helper that both login and this would call into.

That's a genuinely excellent walkthrough — the token hashing, the expiry window, the generic response to prevent enumeration, clearing the fields on use, reusing the signup password-hashing logic, all correct and in the right order. You've clearly internalized the security reasoning, not just the steps.

One gap worth naming: you described the server comparing the incoming hashed token against stored tokens, but didn't say how it finds *which* user document to check against — does it look up by a user ID also embedded in the reset link, or does it have to search all users for a matching hashed token? That changes what the reset link's URL actually needs to contain.

Don't answer that now — just hold it in mind. I'll check it against the real diff once the agent finishes.

Score: you named 5 of the 6 planned files — nice work, especially nailing the token/hash/expiry reasoning in your walkthrough, which is exactly what's in the code.

Here's the one gap: alongside the 6 planned files, the agent also added **`server/middleware/rateLimit.js`**, which wasn't in the plan at all. I'll hold off on what it does for now — we'll come back to it.

---

Let's go through every file so the whole picture is solid, including the ones you already called correctly.

**`server/lib/crypto.js`** (unchanged) — your prediction was right, the agent reused this. It's the library responsible for generating random tokens and hashing things like passwords and now reset tokens. "Hashing" here means a one-way transformation: you can turn `"abc123"` into some scrambled string, but you can't reverse the scrambled string back into `"abc123"`. That's why it's safe to store the *hashed* token in the database — if someone stole the database, they'd have the hash, not the usable token from the email link.

**`server/lib/mailer.js`** (unchanged) — the email-sending library, reused as you predicted. The controller calls into it to actually dispatch the reset link email rather than fiddling with SMTP details itself.

**`server/models/User.js`** — gained two new fields on the user document: something like `resetTokenHash` and `resetTokenExpiry`. This is the storage for "a reset is in progress for this user." No reset is active, these are empty/null.

**`server/controllers/authController.js`** — gained the actual logic for both steps you described: `forgotPassword` (look up user by email, generate token via crypto.js, hash it, save hash+expiry to the user, call mailer.js to send the link, always respond generically) and `resetPassword` (hash the incoming token, find a user whose stored hash matches *and* whose expiry hasn't passed, update their password via crypto.js, clear the reset fields).

**`server/routes/auth.js`** — registered two new endpoints, something like `POST /forgot-password` and `POST /reset-password`, wiring URLs to the controller functions above. You called this one correctly.

**`client/src/api/auth.js`** — gained two new functions, `requestReset(email)` and `confirmReset(token, newPassword)`, each doing a `fetch` to the new server endpoints. You named this one too.

**`client/src/pages/ForgotPassword.jsx`** — new page, email field only, calls `requestReset` on submit, shows the generic success message regardless of whether the email existed.

**`client/src/pages/ResetPassword.jsx`** — new page that reads the token out of the URL (answering the question I left you with last time — worth double-checking how exactly it's read, by query param or route param), shows a new-password form, and calls `confirmReset` on submit.

**`client/src/routes.jsx`** — registered both new pages so they're reachable by URL. You called this correctly too.

**`client/src/pages/Login.jsx`** — gained a "Forgot password?" link pointing at the new ForgotPassword page. You named this correctly as well.

---

Now — in your own words, walk me through the feature end to end one more time, but this time fold in what each file contributes, as if you were explaining it to a teammate who's never seen this codebase. I'll fill in the rate-limiting piece once you're through.

So the flow starts on the login page, which now has a forgot-password link sitting under the form, taking the user to a new ForgotPassword page that's just an email field. That submits through a new requestReset function in the client's auth api wrapper, which hits a new forgot-password route the agent registered in the server's auth routes file, landing in a new forgotPassword function in the auth controller: it looks up the user by email, and regardless of whether it finds one, it generates a token via crypto.js, hashes it, saves the hash and an expiry onto the user document in two new fields the agent added to the User model, and hands the unhashed token off to mailer.js to email as a link, then always returns the same generic message to the client so you can't tell from the response whether that email was registered.

User opens the email, clicks the link, lands on the new ResetPassword page, which pulls the token out of the URL, probably a query param given how little else changed, shows a plain new-password form, and on submit calls a new confirmReset function in the client auth api that posts the token and password to the reset-password route, hitting the resetPassword controller function: it hashes the incoming token, searches for a user whose stored hash matches and whose expiry hasn't passed, and if that succeeds it rehashes the password through crypto.js the same way signup does, saves it, and clears both reset fields on the user so the link is dead afterward. Both new pages got wired into routes.jsx so they're actually reachable, and I'd guess the reset page then just redirects to login rather than logging the user in directly, same reasoning as before, no shared session-issuing helper that I'd seen.

That's complete — every file's role is accounted for correctly, including your reasoning about the query param and the redirect-to-login behavior.

One detail a maintainer would flag: that rate limiter I mentioned earlier sits in front of `forgotPassword` in the route chain, capping how many reset requests can be made per IP or per email in a given window — without it, the endpoint would be an easy target for spamming a user's inbox with reset emails or for brute-forcing the enumeration protection by timing responses at volume.

Worth checking what the actual limit and window are set to.

Now server/middleware/rateLimit.js, the one that was not in the plan. Before I explain it - do you know what Express middleware is?

Yeah, middleware in Express is a function that sits in the request-handling chain before the actual route handler runs, it gets the request, response, and a next callback, and it can inspect or modify the request, short-circuit with its own response, or call next to pass control along. So a rate limiter as middleware would check something like a counter keyed on IP or email before forgotPassword ever runs, and either let the request through or reject it early with a 429 if the caller's over the limit.

Good, that's a solid grasp of middleware, so I won't belabor it.

This particular file keeps an in-memory map of IP address to a list of recent request timestamps, and on each request to `/auth/forgot` it prunes anything older than fifteen minutes and rejects with a 429 once six requests remain in that window — so the same IP can't be used to spam reset emails at an address.

Whether to keep it, tweak the limit, or pull it out entirely is your call — I won't be changing any code here.

That's everything the agent touched. You've now got the full picture of all seven files, including one it added without being asked.

Last one. To change how long a reset link stays valid, from one hour to six, which file do you edit?
That'd be server/controllers/authController.js, wherever forgotPassword sets the expiry timestamp when it saves the token hash to the user.

Confirmed — `server/controllers/authController.js`, in `forgot()`, the line setting `user.resetTokenExpiry = Date.now() + 60 * 60 * 1000`.
